parts.text: A pencil case contains 6 black pens and $n$ blue pens. Ravi takes a pen at random from the pencil case, and then takes a second pen at random. If the first pen is blue, he puts it back into the pencil case before taking the second pen. If the first pen is black, he keeps it and does not put it back. The probability that Ravi takes two black pens is $\frac{1}{7}$. Find $n$.
parts.label: a

parts.text:
A survey records the time, $t$ minutes, that 60 office workers take to travel to work one morning.
$$\begin{array}{|c|c|} \hline \text{Time taken (min)} & \text{Number of workers} \\ \hline 10 \leq t < 20 & 8 \\ \hline 20 \leq t < 30 & 14 \\ \hline 30 \leq t < 40 & 21 \\ \hline 40 \leq t < 50 & 12 \\ \hline 50 \leq t < 60 & 5 \\ \hline \end{array}$$
parts.label: b

subparts.text: Calculate an estimate of the mean time taken.
subparts.label: i

subparts.text: Calculate an estimate of the standard deviation of the times.
subparts.label: ii

parts.text: The members of a bowling club took part in two rounds of a competition, Round A and Round B. The box-and-whisker plots show the scores of the members in each round. Mei Ling scored 150 in both rounds. Comment on whether Mei Ling did better, compared with the other members, in Round A or in Round B.
parts.label: c
parts.answer: In Round A her score of 150 is above the upper quartile (145), so she is in the top 25% of the members; in Round B her score of 150 is below the median (155), so she is in the bottom half. Hence Mei Ling did better in Round A.

figure.description: For part (c) only. Two horizontal box-and-whisker plots drawn one above the other on ONE common horizontal axis labelled 'Score'. The axis runs from 90 to 200, with major tick marks and numbers every 10 (90, 100, 110, ..., 200) and minor tick marks every 5. The upper plot is labelled 'Round A' on its left: lower whisker end (minimum) at 95, box from lower quartile 120 to upper quartile 145, median line inside the box at 135, upper whisker end (maximum) at 175. The lower plot is labelled 'Round B' on its left: minimum at 105, box from lower quartile 130 to upper quartile 165, median line at 155, maximum at 190. Boxes the same height, whiskers as horizontal lines from the box ends to short vertical end marks. No other labels or values written on the plots.

verdict.why: New contexts and sentences. Part (a) turns the event round onto the kept colour, so it leads to a quadratic with a rejected root, and part (c) reverses which plot wins. It is clean and at the right level, but its answer to (a) is the source's n = 9, a coincidence a candidate would notice. The stray [2] after the table also needs removing.
fixes: (a) The answer n = 9 is the same as the source's answer. Change the numbers so the answer differs, e.g. keep 6 black pens and make the probability 1/8: then (n+6)(n+5) = 240, (n-10)(n+21) = 0, n = 10.
(b) Remove the stray [2] printed after the table. The marks belong only on (i) [1] and (ii) [1], and the part total is shown by them.
verdict.key_verdict: The setter's key and the blind examiner agree on every part, and my own working confirms both.

gen_meta.method_note: Source teaches a mixed replacement rule to form an equation for an unknown count, grouped mean/standard deviation from mid-points, and judging one score against the quartiles of two box plots; the twin uses the same three methods, with (a) built on the NON-replaced colour so the equation is a quadratic with one root rejected.

blind_answers.(c): Mei Ling did better in Round A. In Round A, 150 is above the upper quartile (145), so she was in the top 25% of members. In Round B, 150 is below the median (155), so she was in the lower half of members.

gen_meta.originality_note: New contexts (pens in a pencil case, workers' travel times, bowling club rounds), new sentences, new numbers (6 black pens, P = 1/7, five 10-minute classes over 60 workers, box plots on 90–200), and the probability event uses the kept colour rather than the replaced one.

question_text: The drama club at a school is building a two-level step unit for its stage. The unit is a prism. Farid drew Figure $P$, the cross-section of the prism, on a grid of 1 cm squares.

parts.text: On the grid, draw an enlargement of Figure $P$ with a scale factor of $\frac{5}{2}$.
parts.label: a
parts.answer: An L-shaped figure with every side $\frac{5}{2}$ times as long as in Figure $P$: base 15 cm, right side 10 cm, top 5 cm, inner vertical side 5 cm, lower step 10 cm, left side 5 cm.

parts.text: Farid cut a solid foam model of the step unit. The model is a prism whose cross-section is the enlarged figure from part (a), and its volume is $1850$ cm$^{3}$. The length of the model is $w$ cm. Calculate the value of $w$.
parts.label: b

parts.text: The real step unit is geometrically similar to the foam model. Every length on the real unit is $4.8$ times the matching length on the model. The whole outside of the real unit, including the two ends and the base, is to be covered with rubber matting. The matting is sold in rectangular sheets like the one shown in the diagram. When the sheets are cut to shape, $15\%$ of the matting is wasted. Suggest how many sheets of matting the club should buy. Justify your decision and show your calculations clearly.
parts.label: c
parts.answer: 3 sheets (surface area of the real unit $= 25\,920$ cm$^{2}$; each sheet gives $10\,200$ cm$^{2}$ of usable matting; $25\,920 \div 10\,200 \approx 2.54$, rounded up).

figure.description:
Two diagrams.

Diagram 1 (for the stem and part (a)): a square grid of 1 cm squares, 24 squares wide and 12 squares high, with the note '1 cm' marked beside one square. Taking the bottom-left grid point as (0, 0), Figure P is an L-shaped hexagon drawn in a solid line with vertices, in order, at (1, 1), (7, 1), (7, 5), (5, 5), (5, 3), (1, 3), joined back to (1, 1). So its base is 6 squares long, its right side is 4 squares high, its top is 2 squares long, the inner vertical side is 2 squares, the lower step is 4 squares long and the left side is 2 squares high. The label 'Figure P' is written inside the shape. The rest of the grid (to the right of the figure) is left empty for the student's enlargement. No lengths are written on the figure; the student reads them from the grid.

Diagram 2 (for part (c)): a single flat rectangle representing one sheet of rubber matting, drawn in plan view, labelled '1.5 m' along its longer side and '0.8 m' along its shorter side, with the caption 'One sheet of matting'. Nothing else is shown.

verdict.why: Same chain as the source (enlarge on a grid, prism volume for a missing length, surface area scaled by k squared, wastage, round up) in a new context with a new L-shaped cross-section, flat sheets instead of boxes and unrelated numbers, so it is a twin and not the source re-numbered. Numbers are clean and the weight suits 10 marks; a light edit to the wording of (c) would make it read as a school's own question.
fixes: Part (c): say what the 15% is a percentage of, e.g. "15% of each sheet is wasted", so the usable area per sheet is unambiguous.

Part (c): covering the base of a stage step unit with rubber matting is odd; either give a reason (e.g. "so that it does not slip on the stage") or keep "including the two ends and the base" but drop "The whole outside of" to avoid saying it twice.

Part (b): "Farid cut a solid foam model" then "The model is a prism whose cross-section is..." can be one sentence: "Farid makes a solid foam model of the step unit, a prism whose cross-section is the enlarged figure from part (a)."
verdict.key_verdict: The setter's key and the blind examiner agree on every part, and my own working confirms 18.5 and 3 sheets.

gen_meta.method_note: Source: enlarge a cross-section on a grid, use volume = cross-section area × length to find the prism's missing dimension, then scale the model's surface area by k² and divide by the usable material per item after wastage, rounding up. The twin teaches the same chain with an L-shaped step unit, scale factor 5/2, and matting sheets.

blind_answers.(a): Enlarged L-shape with sides 15, 10, 5, 5, 10, 5 cm (base 15, right side 10, top 5, inner vertical 5, lower step 10, left side 5): vertices e.g. (1,1),(16,1),(16,11),(11,11),(11,6),(1,6) taking a copy that fits the grid (area 100 cm^2)
blind_answers.(c): 3 sheets (real cross-section area 2304 cm^2, real length 88.8 cm, cross-section perimeter 240 cm, total surface area 25920 cm^2 = 2.592 m^2; usable per sheet 0.85 x 1.2 = 1.02 m^2; 2.592/1.02 = 2.54, so buy 3 sheets)

question_text:
A bus is travelling along a straight road towards a stretch of roadworks. The diagram shows its speed-time graph over $60$ seconds.
The bus first moves at a steady $12\text{ m/s}$ and covers $240\text{ m}$ before the driver brakes at $t = k$.
It then slows down uniformly at $0.4\text{ m/s}^{2}$ until $t = 40$, when its speed is $w\text{ m/s}$.
It keeps this speed of $w\text{ m/s}$ through the roadworks until $t = 60$.

parts.text: Calculate the value of $k$ and the value of $w$.
parts.label: a

parts.text: On the grid, draw the distance-time graph of the bus for $0 \le t \le 60$.
parts.label: b
parts.answer: Distance-time graph: a straight line from $(0,\ 0)$ to $(20,\ 240)$, a curve of decreasing gradient from $(20,\ 240)$ to $(40,\ 400)$, then a straight line (less steep) from $(40,\ 400)$ to $(60,\ 480)$.

figure.description:
Two separate diagrams, one above the other.

Diagram 1 (given speed-time graph, a sketch, not on a grid). Horizontal axis labelled 'Time ($t$ seconds)', vertical axis labelled 'Speed (m/s)', origin labelled $0$. The graph is three straight segments joined end to end: (1) a horizontal segment at speed $12$ from $t = 0$ to $t = k$; (2) a straight segment sloping downwards from the point $(k,\ 12)$ to the point $(40,\ w)$; (3) a horizontal segment at speed $w$ from $t = 40$ to $t = 60$, where the graph ends. On the vertical axis mark and label only $12$ and $w$ (with $w$ at about one third of the height of $12$). On the horizontal axis mark and label only $k$, $40$ and $60$ (with $k$ at about one third of the way to $60$). Draw dashed vertical guide lines from $(k,\ 12)$, $(40,\ w)$ and $(60,\ w)$ down to the time axis, and a dashed horizontal guide line from $(40,\ w)$ across to the vertical axis. Do not print the values of $k$ or $w$ anywhere.

Diagram 2 (blank grid for the answer). A square grid with horizontal axis labelled 'Time ($t$ seconds)' running from $0$ to $60$, numbered $0, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60$, and vertical axis labelled 'Distance (m)' running from $0$ to $500$, numbered $0, 100, 200, 300, 400, 500$. Fine grid lines every $2$ seconds horizontally and every $20\text{ m}$ vertically, with heavier lines at the numbered values. Nothing is drawn on this grid.

verdict.why: A sound, examination-clean question with a correct key and a clear teacher-voice solution; it tests the same skill by the same method as the source but with a different journey shape (constant, brake, constant, never at rest), a new context and unrelated numbers, so it is a twin and not a re-numbering. It loses one point only for a slightly wordy stem and 'slows down' / 'keeps this speed' phrasing that a light edit would fix.
fixes: Use the exam register for the motion: 'It then decelerates uniformly at 0.4 m/s^2 until t = 40' in place of 'slows down uniformly at', and 'It continues at w m/s until t = 60' in place of 'It keeps this speed of w m/s through the roadworks'.

Tighten the stem so it does not narrate the whole diagram: keep 'The diagram shows the speed-time graph of a bus over 60 seconds', then give only the two facts the graph cannot show (240 m covered at 12 m/s before braking at t = k; deceleration 0.4 m/s^2).
Part (a): 'Find the value of k and the value of w.' is the usual wording for a 2-mark read-off of this kind; 'Calculate' is acceptable but heavier than the working needs.
verdict.key_verdict: No disagreement: the setter's key and the blind examiner match on both parts, and my own working confirms k = 20, w = 4 and the points (20, 240), (40, 400), (60, 480).

gen_meta.method_note: Source: use acceleration and distance = speed × time to find two unknowns on a speed-time graph, then use areas to plot key points and sketch the distance-time graph with the right shape per phase; the twin does the same with a constant–decelerate–constant journey, so the shapes are straight, concave-down curve, straight.

blind_answers.(b): Straight line from (0, 0) to (20, 240) (gradient 12); then a smooth curve, concave down (gradient decreasing from 12 to 4), through (30, 340) to (40, 400); then a straight line from (40, 400) to (60, 480) (gradient 4). Key points: (0,0), (20,240), (40,400), (60,480).

gen_meta.originality_note: New context (a bus slowing for roadworks, not a cyclist), a different journey shape (starts at constant speed, brakes to a lower steady speed, never at rest), new unknowns ($k$ on the time axis, $w$ on the speed axis), fresh numbers and wording.

parts.text: The equation of a circle is $x^2 + y^2 + 6x - 10y + 9 = 0$. By finding the centre and the radius of the circle, decide whether the point $A(1, 9)$ is inside the circle, on the circle or outside the circle.
parts.label: a
parts.answer: $A$ lies outside the circle (centre $(-3, 5)$, radius $5$; distance from centre to $A$ is $\sqrt{32} = 4\sqrt{2} > 5$).

parts.text: A yacht has switched on a distress beacon at a point $C$ out at sea. In the diagram the $x$-axis is a straight coastline and $1$ unit represents $1$ km. Two radio masts on the coastline stand at $M(1, 0)$ and $N(9, 0)$. Both masts pick up the beacon with the same signal strength, which shows that $C$ is the same distance from $M$ as it is from $N$. A patrol boat at $K(-3, 9)$ picks up the beacon along the straight line $L$. The line $L$ is perpendicular to a straight undersea cable whose equation is $y = 2x + 4$.
parts.label: b

subparts.text: Show that the equation of the line $L$ is $x + 2y = 15$.
subparts.label: i
subparts.answer: Shown: gradient of cable $= 2$, so gradient of $L = -\frac{1}{2}$; through $K(-3, 9)$: $y - 9 = -\frac{1}{2}(x + 3)$, i.e. $x + 2y = 15$.

subparts.text: Find the coordinates of $C$.
subparts.label: ii

subparts.text: Hence write down the equation of the circle, centre $C$, on which both masts lie.
subparts.label: iii

subparts.text: The coastguard claims that one circle with centre $C$ can be drawn through $M$, $N$ and $K$. Explain whether the claim is correct.
subparts.label: iv
subparts.answer: Not correct: $CK = \sqrt{80} \neq \sqrt{41}$, so $K$ is not on the circle through $M$ and $N$ with centre $C$.

figure.description: A set of $x$- and $y$-axes with origin $O$, drawn to scale: $x$ from about $-4$ to $11$, $y$ from about $-1$ to $11$. The $x$-axis is labelled 'coastline'. Two points on the $x$-axis are marked with dots and labelled $M(1, 0)$ and $N(9, 0)$. A point in the second quadrant is marked with a dot and labelled $K(-3, 9)$. A straight line labelled 'cable' is drawn with gradient $2$ through $(-2, 0)$ and $(0, 4)$, extending up to about $(3, 10)$; its equation is NOT printed on the diagram. A second straight line labelled $L$ starts at $K(-3, 9)$ and slopes downwards to the right with gradient $-\frac{1}{2}$, crossing the cable at $(1.4, 6.8)$ where a small right-angle mark is drawn, crossing the $y$-axis at $(0, 7.5)$, and continuing through the point $(5, 5)$ to about $(8, 3.5)$. The point $(5, 5)$ on $L$ is marked with a dot and labelled $C$ only (no coordinates shown). No circle is drawn. No other lengths, angles or coordinates are shown.

verdict.why: A sound, correctly keyed question with clean numbers and the same chain as the source (general form to centre and radius, bisector meets a line, radius by distance, third-point check), in a new setting with a perpendicular-line gradient instead of a 45-degree angle, a vertical bisector and the opposite outcome in (a). The story is a close cousin of the source's (two stations hear a signal equally, a third along a line), and the wording needs the light edits above before it reads like a school's paper.
fixes: (b)(iii): change 'Hence write down the equation' to 'Hence find the equation' — 2 marks with a radius to calculate is not a 'write down'.

(b) stem: say outright that C lies on L, e.g. 'The patrol boat at K(-3, 9) detects the beacon in the direction of the straight line L, so C lies on L' — 'picks up the beacon along the straight line L' is loose.
(b) stem: drop the printed '[0]' after the stem; a stem carries no mark bracket.
(b)(iv): 'Explain, with working, whether the claim is correct' so the 1 mark is clearly for the distance comparison, not a bare yes/no.
verdict.key_verdict: The setter's key and the blind examiner agree on every part, and my own working confirms each value; nothing differs.

gen_meta.method_note: Source: centre and radius from the general form, compare the point's distance with the radius; then a centre found where the perpendicular bisector of two points meets a line through a third point, radius by distance, and a distance comparison for the third point. The twin teaches the same chain, with the line's gradient coming from a perpendicular to a given line.

blind_answers.(a): Centre (-3, 5), radius 5. Distance from centre to A = sqrt(32) = 4*sqrt(2) ≈ 5.66 > 5, so A(1, 9) is outside the circle.
blind_answers.(b)(i): Shown: gradient of cable = 2, so gradient of L = -1/2; y - 9 = -1/2 (x + 3) gives x + 2y = 15.
blind_answers.(b)(iv): Claim is incorrect: CK^2 = 8^2 + 4^2 = 80 (CK = 4*sqrt(5) ≈ 8.94), but CM = CN = sqrt(41) ≈ 6.40, so K does not lie on the circle centre C through M and N.

question_text:
Mrs Lim is travelling from Singapore to Kuala Lumpur with her husband, her 67-year-old mother and her 10-year-old son. She can go either by train or by coach. The table below shows the ticket prices for each.
$$\begin{array}{|l|c|l|c|}
\hline
\textbf{Southern Rail} & & \textbf{Starline Coach} & \\
\hline
\text{adult ticket} & \$45 & \text{adult ticket} & \$39 \\
\text{senior ticket} & \$33 & \text{senior ticket} & \$39 \\
\text{child ticket} & \$28 & \text{child ticket} & \$27 \\
\hline
\end{array}$$
Note: child tickets are for ages below 12; senior tickets are for ages 65 and above.

parts.text: Calculate the total cost of the tickets for the family if they travel by Southern Rail.
parts.label: a

parts.text: Calculate the total cost of the tickets for the family if they travel by Starline Coach.

question_text: A school carnival runs a spinner game, and a farm cooperative records the masses of its eggs.

parts.text: At a carnival stall, a player spins two fair spinners at the same time. Spinner $X$ is divided into 5 equal sectors: 2 are green and 3 are orange. Spinner $Y$ is divided into 3 equal sectors: 2 are green and 1 is orange.
parts.label: a

subparts.text: Find the probability that both spinners land on green. Give your answer as a fraction in its simplest form.
subparts.label: i

subparts.text: If both spinners land on green, the player wins a soft toy. If exactly one spinner lands on green, the player is given one more turn and spins both spinners again; the player wins a soft toy if both spinners land on green on this second turn. Otherwise the player wins nothing. Find the probability that the player wins a soft toy. Give your answer as a fraction in its simplest form.
subparts.label: ii

parts.text: The cumulative frequency curve shows the distribution of the masses, in grams, of 160 eggs collected from Farm A.
parts.label: b
parts.answer: (i) median $= 61$ g, IQR $= 7$ g (ii) $234^\circ$ (iii) median decreases by 3 g to 58 g; IQR unchanged at 7 g (iv) not true — the curve does not show individual masses (v) Rahul is incorrect: only 30 eggs, 18.75%, are heavier than 65 g (vi) Farm A eggs heavier on average (median 61 g vs 59 g); Farm A masses more consistent (IQR 7 g vs 13 g)

subparts.text:

(b) the interquartile range.
subparts.label: i

subparts.text: The masses of the 160 eggs are to be displayed in a pie chart. Find the angle of the sector that represents the eggs with a mass between 55 g and 65 g.
subparts.label: ii

subparts.text: The farmer later discovers that the scale was not set to zero, so every mass recorded is 3 g more than the true mass of the egg. State how the median and the interquartile range of the true masses compare with your answers in part (b)(i).
subparts.label: iii
subparts.answer: The median decreases by 3 g (to 58 g); the interquartile range is unchanged (7 g).

subparts.text: Mei Ling looks at the curve and says: "The heaviest egg from Farm A has a mass of exactly 75 g." Explain why she cannot be sure that this is true.
subparts.label: iv
subparts.answer: The curve only shows that all 160 eggs have a mass of at most 75 g; the individual masses are not known, so the heaviest egg may be lighter than 75 g.

subparts.text: Rahul says: "At least 25% of the eggs from Farm A have a mass of more than 65 g." Is Rahul correct? Show your working clearly.
subparts.label: v
subparts.answer: No. Eggs heavier than 65 g $= 160 - 130 = 30$, which is $18.75\% < 25\%$.

subparts.text: The box-and-whisker plot shows the distribution of the masses, in grams, of the eggs collected from Farm B. Make two comparisons between the masses of the eggs from Farm A and Farm B.
subparts.label: vi
subparts.answer: The eggs from Farm A are heavier on average, since the median for Farm A (61 g) is greater than that for Farm B (59 g). The masses of the eggs from Farm A are more consistent, since the interquartile range for Farm A (7 g) is smaller than that for Farm B (13 g).

question_text:
A marine biologist weighs six fish of one species. For each fish, the length is $L$ cm and the mass is $m$ g. The results are shown in the table below.

| $L$ | 12 | 15 | 20 | 25 | 32 | 40 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $m$ | 27.0 | 51.5 | 146 | 226 | 463 | 885 |

It is believed that $m$ and $L$ are related by the formula $m = aL^{n}$, where $a$ and $n$ are constants. One of the masses was recorded wrongly.

parts.text: Explain how a straight line graph can be obtained from the formula $m = aL^{n}$, stating the variables to plot and how $a$ and $n$ can be found from the line.
parts.label: a
parts.answer: $\lg m = n\lg L + \lg a$. Plot $\lg m$ against $\lg L$. Gradient $= n$, vertical intercept $= \lg a$.

parts.text: On the grid, plot $\lg m$ against $\lg L$ and draw a straight line through the points, showing that five of the six fish fit the formula closely.
parts.label: b

parts.text: Using your graph, identify the fish whose mass was recorded wrongly and estimate its correct mass.
parts.label: c

parts.text: Use your graph to estimate the value of $n$.
parts.label: d

figure.description: A blank sheet of graph paper for plotting, with NO axes, labels, scales or points drawn on it. The grid is 14 cm wide and 18 cm tall, ruled in 1 cm major squares (darker lines) each subdivided into 2 mm minor squares (lighter lines). Nothing else is on the figure.

It has a new context, a positive-gradient form and data that does not come from the source's numbers, and the numbers are clean and give a realistic fish law. Only small edits keep it from being paper-ready: (b) gives away the variables that (a) asks for, the solution uses m for two things, and the scale suggestion does not fit the grid.

In the solution to (a), don't write 'Y = mX + c', because m is already the mass. Write 'Y = (gradient)X + (intercept)' or use Y = MX + C.

Fix the suggested vertical scale. lg m from 1.2 to 3.2 does not fit an 18 cm grid at 1 cm to 0.1 (it needs 20 cm). Use lg m from 1.4 to 3.2 at 1 cm to 0.1, and keep lg L from 1.0 to 1.7 at 2 cm to 0.1 across.

question_text:
A metal rain collector hangs from a garden fence. Its open top is the pentagon $PQRST$ shown in the first diagram.
$PQ = 6$ cm, $PT = QR = 4$ cm and $TS = SR = 5$ cm.
Angle $TPQ$ = angle $PQR = 90^\circ$.

parts.text: Show that angle $TSR$ is $73.74^\circ$.
parts.label: i

parts.text: Calculate the area of the open top $PQRST$.
parts.label: ii

parts.text: The second diagram shows the collector. It is an inverted pyramid with vertex $V$, and $N$ is the point on the open top that is vertically above $V$. When full, the collector holds $0.18$ litres of water. Calculate the depth, $VN$, of the collector.
parts.label: iii

parts.text: The collector is full when a small hole is opened at $V$. Water then drains out at a constant rate of $9\text{ cm}^3/\text{s}$ until the collector is empty. On the axes given, sketch the depth of the water against time as the collector empties.
parts.label: iv
parts.answer: Curve starts at $(0,\ 15)$, falls slowly at first and then more and more steeply (the surface gets smaller as the water level drops), reaching $(20,\ 0)$; the collector empties in $180 \div 9 = 20$ s.

figure.description:
Two diagrams side by side, plus a pair of blank axes for part (iv).

Diagram 1 (plane figure): a pentagon PQRST shaped like a house, vertices labelled in anticlockwise order. Use coordinates in cm: P(0, 0) bottom left, Q(6, 0) bottom right, R(6, 4) right, S(3, 8) top (the apex), T(0, 4) left. Sides drawn: PQ, QR, RS, ST, TP. Label PQ as 6 (below the base), PT as 4 (to the left of the left side), QR as 4 (to the right of the right side), TS as 5 and SR as 5 (beside the two sloping sides). Mark right-angle squares at P (angle TPQ) and at Q (angle PQR). Do NOT draw the line TR and do NOT mark any other angle. Not drawn to scale note is not needed; all lengths are in centimetres.

Diagram 2 (solid): an inverted pyramid whose open top is the same pentagon PQRST drawn in perspective as a horizontal face, with the vertex V directly below the top face. Slant edges VP, VQ, VR, VS, VT are drawn (hidden edges dashed). A point N is marked inside the pentagon PQRST, directly above V, and a dashed vertical line joins V to N, with a right-angle mark at N to show VN is perpendicular to the top face. Labels: P, Q, R, S, T at the top vertices, N on the top face, V at the bottom vertex. No lengths are written on Diagram 2.

Axes for part (iv): a blank pair of axes in the first quadrant only, origin labelled 0. Horizontal axis labelled 'Time (s)', vertical axis labelled 'Depth of water (cm)'. No scale, no grid values and no curve drawn.

verdict.why: A true twin: the same chain (angle by trigonometry, ½ab sin C area, pyramid height from volume, depth–time sketch) on a different pentagon with unrelated numbers, a capacity in litres and a draining rather than filling sketch, with clean answers and a clear solution. Stem: drop 'hangs from a garden fence' (it adds nothing) and say 'The first diagram shows the open top of a metal rain collector, the pentagon PQRST.'
Solution (ii): write the triangle's area as '= 12 cm²' or '= 12.0 cm² (3 s.f.)' so the final 36 cm² follows without a rounding question.
verdict.key_verdict: The setter's key and the blind examiner agree on every part; I re-worked each part and the key is correct.

gen_meta.method_note: Source: split an equal-sided pentagon into triangles, get an angle by trigonometry, use ½ab sin C for the area, then pyramid volume for the height and a depth-time sketch for constant flow; the twin does the same chain on a house-shaped pentagon (rectangle + isosceles triangle, right-angled trig for the apex angle, ½ab sin C, pyramid volume from a capacity in litres) and sketches depth against time for draining instead of filling.

question_text:
A tea estate produced 200 batches of tea in one season. Every batch was tasted by two panels of judges, Panel A and Panel B, and each panel gave the batch a score out of 60.
The cumulative frequency curve in Diagram 1 shows the distribution of the scores given by Panel A.

parts.text: For the scores given by Panel A, use the curve to estimate
parts.label: a

subparts.text: the median score,
subparts.label: i

subparts.text: the interquartile range.
subparts.label: ii

parts.text: Two of the batches are picked at random for export. Find the probability that Panel A gave each of them a score of 45 or less.
parts.label: b

parts.text: A batch is labelled 'premium' if its Panel A score is more than $80\%$ of the highest possible score. Estimate the number of premium batches.
parts.label: c

parts.text: The box-and-whisker plot in Diagram 2 shows the distribution of the scores that Panel B gave to the same 200 batches. Estimate the number of batches that Panel B scored between 41 and 46.
parts.label: d

parts.text: Compare the scores given by the two panels in two different ways. Support each comparison with figures.
parts.label: e
parts.answer: Panel B's median ($41$) is higher than Panel A's ($34$), so Panel B gave higher scores in general. Panel B's interquartile range ($10$) is smaller than Panel A's ($18$), so Panel B's scores were less spread out (more consistent).

figure.description:
Two separate diagrams.

Diagram 1 (cumulative frequency curve, titled 'Panel A'): drawn on a square grid. Horizontal axis labelled 'Score', from 0 to 60, numbered at 0, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, with 10 small squares between consecutive numbers (1 small square = 1 score). Vertical axis labelled 'Cumulative frequency', from 0 to 200, numbered at 0, 20, 40, ..., 200, with 10 small squares between consecutive numbers (1 small square = 2 batches). A single smooth S-shaped increasing curve passes exactly through these points (score, cumulative frequency): (0, 0), (10, 6), (20, 24), (25, 50), (30, 80), (34, 100), (40, 134), (43, 150), (45, 160), (48, 176), (50, 184), (55, 196), (60, 200). No points are marked or labelled on the curve and no construction lines are drawn.

Diagram 2 (box-and-whisker plot, titled 'Panel B'): drawn above a horizontal number line labelled 'Score', from 0 to 60, numbered at 0, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, with 10 small divisions between consecutive numbers (1 small division = 1 score). The left whisker starts at 18, the box runs from 36 to 46 with the median line inside it at 41, and the right whisker ends at 58. No values are written on the plot itself; they are read from the number line.

subparts.label: ii

question_text: A craft shop makes a cardboard sleeve to wrap around a flower pot. The sleeve is the curved surface of a frustum and is open at both ends, as shown in Diagram I. The radius of the top rim of the sleeve is 160 mm and the radius of its bottom rim is 100 mm. The vertical height of the sleeve is 250 mm. The sleeve is cut from a flat piece of card. Diagram II shows the shaded piece of card, which is the region between two arcs with the same centre $O$ and the same angle $\theta$ at $O$.

parts.label: a

parts.text: The shorter arc in Diagram II forms the bottom rim of the sleeve and has radius $r_1$ mm. The longer arc forms the top rim and has radius $(r_1 + h)$ mm. Show that $r_1 = 428.5$, correct to 1 decimal place.

parts.text: Hence, find the angle $\theta$, in degrees.
parts.label: c

figure.description: Two diagrams side by side, not drawn to scale. The top rim's radius is drawn as a line from the centre of the top ellipse to its edge, labelled 160 mm. The bottom rim's radius is drawn as a line from the centre of the bottom ellipse to its edge, labelled 100 mm. A dashed vertical line joins the two centres, labelled 250 mm. One slanted side edge (from the bottom rim up to the top rim) is labelled h mm. Caption: Diagram I. Diagram II: the flat net of the sleeve — a shaded annular sector (the region between two concentric arcs). The centre O is at the bottom of the diagram; two straight lines go up from O, opening at an angle marked θ at O. A short unshaded arc of radius r₁ mm and a longer arc of radius (r₁ + h) mm are both centred at O and both cut off by the two straight lines; only the region between the two arcs is shaded. Label the distance from O to the inner arc along one straight line as r₁ mm, and the length of the shaded edge along that same line (from the inner arc to the outer arc) as h mm. parts.text: On the axes provided, sketch the graph of $y = 4\cos\left(\frac{\pi x}{2}\right) - 1$ for $0 \leq x \leq 6$.
parts.label: b

Vertical axis labelled $y$, from $-6$ to $4$, with a tick and label at every integer $-6, -5, \dots, 3, 4$ (one major grid square per unit), arrow at the top. Origin labelled $O$. No curve drawn — the grid is empty.

parts.text:
Figure 1 shows two identical triangular flags pinned along a straight rail $PRT$. Triangle $PQR$ is congruent to triangle $RST$, with $PQ = RS$, $QR = ST$ and $PR = RT$. The points $Q$ and $S$ are on the same side of the rail.
Complete the sentences below to show that the edge $PQ$ is parallel to the edge $RS$.
Since the triangles are congruent, angle $QPR$ = angle ________ .
These two angles are in the positions of a pair of ________ angles on the straight line $PRT$.
Since they are equal, $PQ$ is parallel to $RS$.
parts.label: a

parts.text:
Figure 2 shows a triangular frame $LMN$. A rope joins the point $X$ on $LM$ to the point $Y$ on $LN$. Triangle $LMN$ is similar to triangle $LYX$.
It is given that $LX = 4$ cm, $XM = 11$ cm and $LY = 5$ cm.
Calculate the length of $YN$.
parts.label: b

figure.description:
Two separate diagrams, labelled Figure 1 and Figure 2.

Figure 1: A horizontal straight line segment with three points on it, from left to right $P$, $R$, $T$, where $R$ is the midpoint of $PT$ ($PR = RT$). Above the line, point $Q$ is joined to $P$ and to $R$, forming triangle $PQR$. Above the line, point $S$ is joined to $R$ and to $T$, forming triangle $RST$. Triangle $RST$ is an exact copy of triangle $PQR$ slid to the right along the line, so $RS$ is parallel to $PQ$ and $ST$ is parallel to $QR$. The triangles are scalene, not right-angled and not isosceles: for example $PR = 6$ units, $PQ = 5$ units, $QR = 4$ units (these lengths are NOT shown). Label only the five points $P$, $Q$, $R$, $S$, $T$. No lengths, no angle marks, no tick marks and no parallel arrows are shown. Do not join $Q$ to $S$.

Figure 2: A triangle $LMN$ with $L$ at the top, $M$ at the bottom left and $N$ at the bottom right. $LM = 15$ cm and $LN = 12$ cm. Point $X$ lies on side $LM$ with $LX = 4$ cm and $XM = 11$ cm. Point $Y$ lies on side $LN$ with $LY = 5$ cm, so $Y$ is a little lower down its side than $X$ is on its side. A straight line segment joins $X$ to $Y$; $XY$ is NOT parallel to $MN$ (it slopes downwards from left to right). Angle $LXY$ equals angle $LNM$ and angle $LYX$ equals angle $LMN$, but no angle marks are drawn. Labels shown: the points $L$, $M$, $N$, $X$, $Y$; the length '4 cm' beside $LX$, '11 cm' beside $XM$ and '5 cm' beside $LY$. The length $YN$ is not labelled.

verdict.why: Key is correct and the question tests the same two skills by the same method, with a new configuration (translated triangles giving corresponding rather than alternate angles), new letters and unrelated numbers, so it is not the source re-numbered. The context wording in (a) is slightly laboured, which a light edit fixes.
fixes: (a) Replace the second sentence 'These two angles are in the positions of a pair of ________ angles on the straight line PRT.' with the plainer 'These two angles are a pair of ________ angles.' — 'in the positions of' is not exam phrasing.
(a) Use 'side' rather than 'edge' for PQ and RS ('show that PQ is parallel to RS'), as a school paper would.
(b) Drop the rope and frame wording or keep it to one clause: 'In Figure 2, X lies on LM and Y lies on LN. Triangle LMN is similar to triangle LYX.'
verdict.key_verdict: The setter's key and the blind examiner agree on both parts, and my own working confirms angle SRT / corresponding and YN = 7 cm.

gen_meta.method_note: Source: read equal angles off the vertex order of congruent triangles to justify parallel lines by completing blanks, then pair sides by the vertex order of two similar triangles sharing a vertex (reversed orientation) and subtract to get a segment; the twin does both the same way.

blind_answers.(b): YN = 7 cm (LM = 15, LM/LY = LN/LX = 3, so LN = 12, YN = 12 - 5 = 7)

gen_meta.originality_note: New situations (two flags slid along a rail giving corresponding rather than alternate angles; a frame with a rope), new letters and sentences, and new lengths 4, 11, 5 giving 7 cm, with the whole side built on the other arm of the triangle.

parts.text: In the diagram, $PQ$ is parallel to $ST$. $\angle PQR = 116^{\circ}$ and $\angle RST = 31^{\circ}$. Stating your reasons clearly, find the reflex angle $QRS$.
parts.label: a

parts.text: Two laser pointers are placed at $H$ and $K$ on a straight stage floor $GL$, where $G$, $H$, $K$ and $L$ lie on the floor in that order. The pointer at $H$ shines a straight beam towards $M$ and the pointer at $K$ shines a straight beam towards $N$. $\angle MHK = 71^{\circ}$ and $\angle NKH = 109^{\circ}$. Stating your reasons clearly, explain whether the two beams will meet.
parts.label: b
parts.answer: The beams will not meet: $\angle NKL = 180^{\circ} - 109^{\circ} = 71^{\circ}$ (adj. $\angle$s on a str. line) $= \angle MHK$, so $HM \parallel KN$ (corr. $\angle$s equal), and parallel lines never meet.

figure.description:
Two separate diagrams, one for each part.
Diagram for (a): two horizontal parallel lines, each marked with a single arrowhead to show they are parallel. Top line: P on the left, Q on the right (segment PQ ends at Q). Bottom line: S on the left, T on the right (segment ST, T to the right of S). Point R lies between the two lines, below and slightly to the right of Q. Segment QR runs from Q down to the right, steeply (about 64° below the horizontal). Segment RS runs from R down to the left to S, shallowly (31° above the horizontal at S). So the path Q-R-S forms a zig-zag with the bend at R pointing to the right. Label the angle at Q between QP and QR as 116° (the obtuse angle on the left/lower side of Q, inside the zig-zag). Label the angle at S between SR and ST as 31° (the acute angle at S, between SR going up-right and ST going right). Mark the reflex angle QRS at R with an arc on the RIGHT side of R (the outside of the bend), labelled with a question mark or no value. Suggested coordinates: P(-3, 2), Q(0, 2), R(0.98, 0), S(-2.35, -2), T(3, -2). No other lines are drawn.
Diagram for (b): a horizontal straight line representing the stage floor with points G, H, K, L marked on it from left to right (G at the left end, L at the right end, H and K between, with HK about 4 units long). From H a straight beam (a line segment ending in an arrowhead) rises up to the right to M, making an angle of 71° with HK; label this angle 71° between HM and HK on the right side of H. From K a straight beam rises up to the right to N, also leaning to the right; label the obtuse angle between KN and KH (on the left side of KN, towards H) as 109°. The beams are NOT marked as parallel. Suggested coordinates: G(-1, 0), H(0, 0), K(4, 0), L(6, 0), M(1.3, 3.8), N(5.3, 3.8).

verdict.why: The twin tests the same two sub-skills by the same methods (auxiliary parallel through the bend; a converse angle property to decide parallelism) with a new layout, a reflex angle instead of the obtuse one, new numbers and a new context for (b), so it does not read as the source. Clean numbers, correct key and a teacher-voice solution; only a light wording edit in (b) separates it from a real Sec 1 question.
fixes: In (b), say in the text that M and N lie on the same side of the floor GL (e.g. 'both beams shine upwards above the floor'), so the question does not rely on the diagram alone for the converse to apply.

In (b)'s solution, write the reason in the standard converse form, e.g. 'HM // KN (corr. ∠s are equal)', and optionally note the co-interior route (71° + 109° = 180°) as an alternative after the working.
verdict.key_verdict: No disagreement: the setter's key (265°; beams parallel, never meet) matches the blind examiner on both parts, and both are correct.

gen_meta.method_note: Source finds the angle at a zig-zag bend between two parallel lines with an auxiliary parallel (alt./int. angles), then decides by a converse angle property whether two launched paths are parallel; the twin does the same: an auxiliary line through the bend giving alt. + int. angles summed for a reflex angle, then the converse of corresponding angles to show two beams are parallel.

blind_answers.(a): Reflex angle QRS = 265°. Reasoning: draw a line through R parallel to PQ and ST. Angle between RQ and this line = 180° - 116° = 64° (co-interior angles, PQ // line through R). Angle between RS and this line = 31° (alternate angles, ST // line through R). So angle QRS = 64° + 31° = 95°, and reflex angle QRS = 360° - 95° = 265° (angles at a point).
blind_answers.(b): No, the beams will not meet (they are parallel). Angle MHK + angle NKH = 71° + 109° = 180°. These are co-interior (allied) angles on the same side of transversal HK, and they add up to 180°, so HM is parallel to KN. Parallel lines never meet.

gen_meta.originality_note: New letters and layout (bend pointing right, reflex angle asked instead of the obtuse one), new numbers 116° and 31° giving 265°, and a new context for (b): laser beams on a stage floor decided by corresponding angles (71°, 109°) instead of drones decided by interior angles.

question_text: Two Venn diagrams are drawn below. In each one the rectangle stands for the universal set $\xi$.

parts.text: Diagram 1 shows two overlapping sets $P$ and $Q$. Shade, on Diagram 1, the region $(P \cup Q')'$.
parts.label: a
parts.answer: Only the part of circle $Q$ that lies outside circle $P$ is shaded, i.e. $P' \cap Q$.

parts.text: In Diagram 2, part of the Venn diagram for sets $C$ and $D$ has been shaded. Write down, in set notation, the region that is shaded.
parts.label: b

figure.description:
Two separate Venn diagrams side by side, each with its caption underneath: 'Diagram 1' on the left and 'Diagram 2' on the right.

Diagram 1 (for part (a), to be shaded by the student): a rectangle with the label $\xi$ just inside its top-left corner. Inside the rectangle are two circles of equal size that overlap in the middle, forming a lens-shaped common region. The left circle is labelled $P$ (label placed just above the left circle, inside the rectangle) and the right circle is labelled $Q$ (label just above the right circle). Nothing is shaded anywhere in Diagram 1. There is clear empty space between the circles and the rectangle on all sides.

Diagram 2 (for part (b), already shaded): a rectangle of the same size with the label $\xi$ just inside its top-left corner. Inside are two circles of equal size that overlap in the middle. The left circle is labelled $C$ and the right circle is labelled $D$ (labels just above each circle). Shading: the whole rectangle is shaded EXCEPT the lens-shaped overlap of the two circles. That is, three regions are shaded with the same light grey hatching — the part of circle $C$ outside circle $D$, the part of circle $D$ outside circle $C$, and all the space inside the rectangle but outside both circles. The lens-shaped overlap of $C$ and $D$ is left white (unshaded). The outlines of both circles and the rectangle stay clearly visible, and the labels are not covered by the shading.

verdict.why: A correct, in-syllabus 2-mark question that goes both ways between notation and region like the source, with different expressions and different answer regions (a single crescent; everything but the overlap), so it is not the source re-lettered. The wording is slightly more explanatory than a real paper and (b) is a touch more routine than the source's A' ∪ B, hence 4 rather than 5.
fixes: Drop the opening sentence 'In each one the rectangle stands for the universal set ξ' — a school paper lets the ξ label on the diagram say this; start directly with part (a).
Tighten (a) to the standard register: 'On Diagram 1, shade the region which represents (P ∪ Q')'.'
Tighten (b) to 'Use set notation to describe the shaded region in Diagram 2.' — 'part of the Venn diagram ... has been shaded' is wordier than a real paper.
In the key for (a), state the condition for the mark: the lens P ∩ Q and the region outside both circles must be left unshaded.
verdict.key_verdict: The setter's key and the blind examiner agree on both parts, and my own working confirms the key is right.

gen_meta.method_note: The source goes both ways between set notation and a Venn region (shade the complement of a compound set; name a pre-shaded region); the twin does the same — (a) shade a complement by building the bracket first, (b) name a shaded region by spotting its unshaded complement.

blind_answers.(a): (P ∪ Q')' = P' ∩ Q, so shade the part of circle Q that is outside P (the crescent of Q only, excluding the lens P ∩ Q; nothing else shaded)

gen_meta.originality_note: New sets and expressions — (a) asks for the complement of a union, giving a single crescent, and (b) shades everything except the overlap, giving $(C \cap D)'$; new letters, two captioned diagrams and freshly worded sentences.

question_text: A carpenter cuts a triangular wooden panel $ABC$ in which angle $ABC = 90^{\circ}$, as shown in Diagram 1. The upright edge $BC$ is $20$ cm long and the sloping edge $AC$ is $29$ cm long.

parts.text: Find the length of the bottom edge $AB$.
parts.label: a

parts.text: Calculate the angle that the sloping edge $AC$ makes with the bottom edge $AB$.
parts.label: b

parts.text: The carpenter glues a second triangular panel $BCD$ onto the edge $BC$, on the other side of $BC$ from $A$, as shown in Diagram 2. In this panel, $BD = 48$ cm and $CD = 52$ cm. The carpenter says that the two bottom edges $AB$ and $BD$ now form one straight edge $ABD$. Show, with clear working, that the carpenter is correct.
parts.label: c
parts.answer: $BC^2 + BD^2 = 20^2 + 48^2 = 2704 = 52^2 = CD^2$, so angle $CBD = 90^{\circ}$ (converse of Pythagoras' theorem). Angle $ABD = 90^{\circ} + 90^{\circ} = 180^{\circ}$, so $ABD$ is a straight edge.

figure.description:
Two separate diagrams side by side, labelled 'Diagram 1' and 'Diagram 2', not drawn to scale.

Diagram 1: a right-angled triangle $ABC$. $B$ is the bottom-right vertex, $A$ is the bottom-left vertex, $C$ is directly above $B$. $AB$ is horizontal, $BC$ is vertical. A small square right-angle marker at $B$ between $AB$ and $BC$. Side $BC$ is labelled '20 cm' (on its right). Side $AC$ (the sloping hypotenuse from bottom-left up to top-right) is labelled '29 cm'. Side $AB$ has NO length label. No angles are marked other than the right angle at $B$.

Diagram 2: the same triangle $ABC$ as in Diagram 1 (same position, same labels '20 cm' on $BC$ and '29 cm' on $AC$, same right-angle marker at $B$ on the $A$ side only), with a second triangle $BCD$ attached to the right of $BC$, sharing the side $BC$. $D$ is at the bottom right, to the right of $B$, roughly level with $A$ and $B$, and further from $B$ than $A$ is (BD is clearly longer than AB). Side $BD$ is labelled '48 cm' (below it). Side $CD$ (sloping from $C$ down to $D$) is labelled '52 cm'. Do NOT put a right-angle marker in triangle $BCD$ at $B$, and do NOT draw anything that states $ABD$ is straight (no single line label spanning $A$ to $D$). Vertices labelled $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$.

verdict.why: Same three steps as the source (Pythagoras for a leg, one trig ratio for an acute angle, converse of Pythagoras on an attached triangle to reach 180 degrees) in a fresh carpenter context with new sentences, unrelated integer triples (20-21-29, 20-48-52) and the angle taken at the other acute vertex. Register, weight for 7 marks, Sec 2 scope and clean numbers all match a school paper, and the solution shows the method one step a line with a clear Answer line.
verdict.key_verdict: The setter's key and the blind examiner agree on every part, and my own working confirms 21 cm, 43.6 degrees and the converse-of-Pythagoras argument.

gen_meta.method_note: Source: Pythagoras for a missing leg, one trig ratio for an acute angle, then the converse of Pythagoras on an attached triangle to get a second right angle and add to 180°; the twin walks the same three steps on a carpenter's panel with a second panel glued on.

blind_answers.(b): tan(angle CAB) = 20/21, so angle CAB = 43.6 degrees (3 s.f.)
blind_answers.(c): In triangle BCD: BC^2 + BD^2 = 20^2 + 48^2 = 400 + 2304 = 2704 = 52^2 = CD^2, so by the converse of Pythagoras' theorem angle CBD = 90 degrees. Angle ABC + angle CBD = 90 + 90 = 180 degrees, and A and D are on opposite sides of BC, so ABD is a straight line. Shown.

gen_meta.originality_note: New context (carpenter's wooden panels and a claim to justify), new triples 20-21-29 and 20-48-52 in place of the source's 14-48-50 and 10.5-14-17.5, the angle asked for is at the other acute vertex via sine, and all sentences are freshly written.

question_text:
The universal set and two of its subsets are defined as follows.
$\xi=\{x:x\text{ is an integer and }11\leq x\leq 24\}$
$P=\{x:x\text{ is a multiple of }3\}$
$Q=\{x:x\text{ is a multiple of }4\}$

parts.text: Write down the value of $n(P')$.
parts.label: a

parts.text: List the elements of $P\cap Q'$.
parts.label: b

parts.text: The Venn diagram shows the sets $\xi$, $P$ and $Q$. On the diagram, shade the region which represents $(P\cup Q)\cap (P\cap Q)'$.
parts.label: c
parts.answer: Shaded region: the part of $P$ outside $Q$ and the part of $Q$ outside $P$. The overlap and the region outside both circles are left unshaded.

figure.description: A blank Venn diagram for the student to shade. A large rectangle, with the label $\xi$ just inside its top-left corner. Inside the rectangle, two circles of equal size overlap in the middle, so that there are four separate regions: left circle only, the overlap, right circle only, and the space inside the rectangle outside both circles. The left circle is labelled $P$ above its top-left edge and the right circle is labelled $Q$ above its top-right edge. No elements, numbers or shading appear anywhere in the diagram. Leave clear space around the circles inside the rectangle so that the outside region can be seen.

verdict.why: Same three one-mark tasks (count, list a compound set, shade a compound region from the notation) on a new universal set with new set definitions, a different count, a different listed set and a different region, so it does not read as the source re-numbered. The register, the mark weight, the clean numbers and the step-by-step solution with a bold Answer line would sit in a school's E Math Paper 1 as written.
verdict.key_verdict: The setter's key and the blind examiner agree on all three parts, and my own working confirms each.

blind_answers.(c): Shade the left-circle-only region (P only) and the right-circle-only region (Q only); leave the overlap P∩Q and the region outside both circles unshaded.

parts.text: The floor of a glasshouse is a regular octagon $ABCDEFGH$ with centre $O$. Each side of the octagon is $2k$ metres long.
parts.label: a

subparts.text: Show that triangle $OAB$ has area $k^2\tan 67.5^{\circ}$ square metres.
subparts.label: i

subparts.text: Hence calculate the area of the floor when $k = 2.5$.
subparts.label: ii

parts.text: The glasshouse has eight vertical glass walls, one standing on each side of the floor, and every wall is $3$ m high. The roof is made of eight glass triangles that meet at a point $T$, which is vertically above $O$. $P$ is the top corner of the walls that is vertically above $A$.
parts.label: b

subparts.text: It is given that $AB = 5$ m and that the roof edge $PT$ is $7.5$ m long. Calculate $OT$, the height of the top of the glasshouse above the floor.
subparts.label: i

subparts.text: Calculate the volume of air inside the glasshouse.
subparts.label: ii

subparts.text: An architect builds a geometrically similar model of the glasshouse in which each wall is $6$ cm high. Calculate the volume of the model, giving your answer in cubic centimetres.
subparts.label: iii

figure.description:
Two diagrams side by side, not to scale.

Diagram 1 (plan view of the floor): a regular octagon with vertices labelled $A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H$ in order anticlockwise, with $AB$ as the horizontal bottom side ($A$ bottom-left, $B$ bottom-right). The centre is marked with a dot and labelled $O$. Straight lines $OA$ and $OB$ are drawn, so triangle $OAB$ is visible. The side $AB$ is labelled $2k$. No angles are marked.

Diagram 2 (3-D view of the glasshouse): the same regular octagon $ABCDEFGH$ drawn in perspective as the floor, with $O$ marked at its centre. From each of the eight vertices a vertical edge of equal height rises to a second, identical octagon directly above the floor (the top of the walls); hidden edges are dashed. The vertical edge at $A$ is labelled $3$ and its top end is labelled $P$. A point $T$ lies vertically above $O$, higher than the top of the walls; straight roof edges join $T$ to each of the eight top corners. The roof edge $PT$ is labelled $7.5$. The floor side $AB$ is labelled $5$. A dashed vertical line joins $O$ to $T$. The other top corners are not labelled. All lengths are in metres.

verdict.why: The key is right throughout and the question tests the same chain (regular polygon split into isosceles triangles, a vertical right-angled triangle, prism + pyramid, cube of the length ratio with a unit change) in a new setting with new numbers and a real change in (b)(i) — a roof edge at a corner instead of a slant height at a midpoint. It would sit in a school paper after light wording edits; (b)(i) is slightly over-weight for 3 marks.
fixes: (b)(i) is heavier than the source's 3 marks: the candidate must find OA by trigonometry, apply Pythagoras in triangle TNP and then add the wall height. Either add a lead-in ('Show that OA = 6.53 m, correct to 3 significant figures') or accept it as a demanding 3 marks.
(b)(ii): 'the volume of air inside the glasshouse' → 'the volume of the glasshouse'.
(b): 'P is the top corner of the walls that is vertically above A' → 'P is the point at the top of the walls vertically above A'.
(b)(i): 'It is given that AB = 5 m and that the roof edge PT is 7.5 m long' → 'Given that AB = 5 m and PT = 7.5 m, calculate the height, OT, of the glasshouse.'
verdict.key_verdict: No part differs: the setter's key and the blind examiner agree on all five parts, and my own working confirms each value.

gen_meta.method_note: Source: split a regular polygon into isosceles triangles at the centre (angle 360°/n, base angle, tan for the perpendicular height), then Pythagoras in a vertical right-angled triangle for the roof height, prism + pyramid volume, and the cube of the length scale factor with a m to cm conversion; the twin teaches the same chain on a regular octagon with walls and a pyramid roof.

blind_answers.(a)(i): shown: angle AOB = 360/8 = 45 deg, so the angle between the apothem and OA is 22.5 deg; the apothem = k/tan 22.5 = k tan 67.5; area = 1/2 x 2k x k tan 67.5 = k^2 tan 67.5

parts.text: Diagram 1 shows the design of a school badge. $OPQ$ is a sector of a circle with centre $O$ and radius 16 cm. A circle with centre $C$ and radius 6 cm lies inside the sector. It touches $OP$ at $T$, $OQ$ at $U$ and the arc $PQ$ at $K$. Find
parts.label: a

subparts.text: $\angle POQ$ in radians,
subparts.label: i

subparts.text: the area of the shaded region, which is bounded by the line $TP$, the arc $PK$ and the minor arc $KT$.
subparts.label: ii

parts.text: Diagram 2 shows two circles which intersect at $M$ and $N$. $P$ and $R$ are points on the first circle, and $Q$ and $S$ are points on the second circle, such that $PMQ$ and $RNS$ are straight lines. Show, stating your reasons clearly, that $PR$ is parallel to $QS$.
parts.label: b

figure.description:
Two separate diagrams, labelled Diagram 1 and Diagram 2.

Diagram 1: A sector $OPQ$ of a circle, centre $O$ at the bottom, radius 16 cm, opening upwards and symmetrical about the vertical line through $O$. Angle $POQ$ is about 73.7° (1.287 rad) — do NOT label the angle. $P$ is the top-left end of the arc, $Q$ the top-right end. Draw the radii $OP$ and $OQ$ and the arc $PQ$. Inside the sector draw a circle, centre $C$, radius 6 cm, with $C$ on the line of symmetry 10 cm from $O$. This circle touches $OP$ at $T$ (8 cm from $O$ along $OP$), touches $OQ$ at $U$ (8 cm from $O$ along $OQ$), and touches the arc $PQ$ at $K$, the midpoint of the arc, vertically above $C$. Mark the points $O$, $P$, $Q$, $C$, $T$, $U$, $K$ with their letters. Draw the radius $CT$ as a thin line. Label the length $OP$ as 16 cm and the length $CT$ as 6 cm. parts.text:
A garden $OAB$ is in the shape of a sector of a circle with centre $O$ and radius $9$ m.
The angle $AOB$ is $1.2$ radians.
The point $C$ lies on the straight edge $OB$ such that $OC = 4$ m.

subparts.label: i

figure.description:
TWO separate diagrams, neither drawn to scale.

Diagram for (a): A circle with centre O (dot, labelled O). Points on the circle: P at the upper-left (about 148 degrees measured anticlockwise from the positive x-direction), Q at the upper-right (about 32 degrees), R on the minor arc PQ near the top of the circle, slightly left of the highest point (about 110 degrees), and S on the major arc at the lower right (about 292 degrees, i.e. below O and a little to the right). Draw the tangents TP and TQ, the straight line OT, the chord PQ, and mark M where OT crosses PQ (M lies between O and T; PQ is horizontal and OT is vertical). Also draw the radii OP, OQ and OS, the chords PR and RQ, and the chords PS and QS. Label the angle PTQ at T as 64°. Label the angle QPS at P (between chords PQ and PS) as 50°. Labels: O, P, Q, R, S, T, M.

Diagram for (b): A sector OAB of a circle with centre O. O is the vertex on the left; OB runs horizontally to the right from O; OA runs up and to the right from O, making an angle of 1.2 rad (about 69 degrees) with OB; the arc AB joins A to B, bulging away from O. Mark 1.2 rad at O. Mark OA = 9 m. Point C lies on OB with OC = 4 m and CB = 5 m (mark OC = 4 m). Draw the straight line AC. Shade the region ABC bounded by the arc AB, the segment BC and the line CA (the part of the sector NOT in triangle OAC). Labels: O, A, B, C.

It uses a new figure, a garden context and new numbers, and its answers are clean and correct. Only the sub-part lettering and the stray mark tags stand between it and a real school question.

In the (a)(i) solution, give the reason for angle PTM = angle QTM as the standard wording, e.g. '(tangents from ext. pt: OT bisects ∠PTQ)', so a marker sees a recognised property and not a claim that seems to assume what it proves.

question_text: Three identical solid bronze balls rest in a rectangular tray $PQRS$. Diagram 1 shows the view from directly above. $A$, $B$ and $C$ are the centres of the balls, and each ball has radius $5$ cm. The balls with centres $A$ and $B$ touch each other, and both touch the side $SR$. The ball with centre $A$ touches the side $PS$ and the ball with centre $B$ touches the side $QR$. The third ball, with centre $C$, touches both of the other balls and the side $PQ$.

parts.text: Find the volume of one bronze ball.
parts.label: a

parts.text: Show that the width $PS$ of the tray is $18.66$ cm, correct to two decimal places.
parts.label: b
parts.answer: Shown: $AC = 10$ cm, half of $AB = 5$ cm, so distance from $C$ to $AB$ $= \sqrt{10^{2} - 5^{2}} = \sqrt{75}$ cm, and $PS = 5 + \sqrt{75} + 5 = 18.6602\ldots \approx 18.66$ cm.

parts.text: A craftsman melts all three balls and uses all the bronze to cast one solid cone, shown in Diagram 2. The base radius of the cone is $\frac{2}{3}$ of its height. Calculate the height, $h$, of the cone.
parts.label: c

parts.text: Calculate the slant height, $l$, of the cone.
parts.label: d

Two diagrams side by side, labelled 'Diagram 1' and 'Diagram 2'.

Diagram 1 (top view): a rectangle $PQRS$ with $P$ top-left, $Q$ top-right, $R$ bottom-right, $S$ bottom-left. The rectangle is 20 units long ($PQ$ and $SR$, horizontal) and about 18.66 units wide ($PS$ and $QR$, vertical); do NOT print these two lengths on the diagram. Inside are three equal circles of radius 5 units. Taking $S$ as the origin: the circle with centre $A$ is at $(5, 5)$, touching side $PS$ and side $SR$; the circle with centre $B$ is at $(15, 5)$, touching side $QR$ and side $SR$; these two circles touch each other at $(10, 5)$. The third circle, with centre $C$, is at $(10, 13.66)$, sitting above and between the other two, touching both of them and touching the top side $PQ$ at its midpoint; it does not touch $PS$ or $QR$. Mark each centre with a small dot and label it $A$, $B$, $C$. Draw one radius in the circle with centre $A$ (from $A$ horizontally left to side $PS$) and label it '5 cm'. No other lengths are shown.

Diagram 2: a solid right circular cone standing on its circular base, apex at the top. The base is drawn as an ellipse (back half dashed). A dashed vertical line from the apex to the centre of the base is labelled $h$, with a right-angle mark at the centre of the base. A dashed radius from the centre of the base to the right-hand edge of the base is drawn but not given a number. The right-hand slanted edge from the apex to the edge of the base is labelled $l$. question_text: A water dispenser uses paper cups in the shape of an open cone. Each cup has a circular rim of radius $3.5$ cm and holds exactly $49\pi\,\text{cm}^{3}$ of water when filled to the rim.

parts.text: A cup is slit in a straight line from its tip $V$ to a point $P$ on the rim and pressed flat. The flattened paper is a sector $VPQ$ of a circle with centre $V$, as shown in Diagram 1. Calculate the angle $y^{\circ}$ of this sector.
parts.label: a

parts.text: A solid wooden fishing float is carved as a cone, geometrically similar to the paper cup, with a solid hemisphere fixed onto its circular base. The base of the cone and the flat face of the hemisphere have the same radius. The slant edge of the cone on the float is $7.5$ cm, as shown in Diagram 2. Calculate the volume of the float.
parts.label: b

figure.description:
Two separate diagrams side by side, each with its caption underneath.

Diagram 1 (caption 'Diagram 1'): on the left, an open hollow cone drawn with its tip pointing DOWN (a paper cup). The tip is labelled V. The open circular rim at the top is drawn as an ellipse; a radius of the rim is drawn as a dashed horizontal line from the centre of the rim to the right-hand edge and labelled '3.5 cm'. The right-hand end of the rim is labelled P. No height and no slant length are marked on the cone. An arrow points from the cone to the right, to a flat sector of a circle. The sector has its centre labelled V at the bottom, two straight edges VP and VQ of equal length going up to the left (Q) and up to the right (P), and a curved arc joining Q to P at the top. The angle at V between VQ and VP is marked with a small arc and labelled y° (it is an obtuse angle, drawn at about 100°). No lengths are marked on the sector.

Diagram 2 (caption 'Diagram 2'): a solid made of a cone with its tip pointing DOWN and a hemisphere sitting on top of the cone's circular base, dome upwards, so the widest part of the solid is the common circle where the two meet (drawn as an ellipse, back half dashed). The hemisphere and the cone have the same radius at that circle. The slant edge of the cone on the right-hand side, from the tip up to the common circle, is labelled '7.5 cm'. No radius and no height are marked. The cone in Diagram 2 has the same proportions as the cone in Diagram 1 (radius : height : slant = 7 : 24 : 25) but is drawn smaller.

verdict.why: Same chain as the source (volume to height to slant height to sector angle, then a similar cone plus hemisphere) in a new setting with new sentences and clean 7:24:25 numbers that are not a scaling of the source's, and the solution shows the method one step a line. Only light wording edits ('slant edge', the phrasing of what to calculate in (a)) separate it from a real school question.
fixes: In (b) and on Diagram 2, say 'slant height' instead of 'slant edge' — it is the syllabus term and the one the candidate needs to match with part (a).
End (a) with 'Calculate the value of y.' (or 'Calculate angle PVQ.') rather than 'Calculate the angle y° of this sector.'
In the stem, 'in the shape of an open cone' reads better as 'in the shape of a hollow cone, open at the rim'; 'pressed flat' could be 'opened out flat' to match the usual wording for a net.
verdict.key_verdict: The setter's key and the blind examiner agree on both parts, and my own working confirms 100.8° and 52.6 cm^3.

gen_meta.method_note: Source: cone volume gives the height, Pythagoras gives the slant height, rim circumference = arc length gives the sector angle; then a similar cone is scaled and added to a hemisphere. The twin teaches the same chain — volume to height to slant to sector angle, then similar-cone scaling plus hemisphere volume.

parts.text: Find $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left[\ln(\cos 2x)\right]$, giving your answer in terms of a single trigonometric function.
parts.label: a

parts.text: The diagram shows the curve $y = -2\tan 2x$ for $0 \le x < \dfrac{\pi}{4}$, which starts at the origin $O$. The horizontal line $y = -2$ meets the curve at the point $Q$. The vertical line through $Q$ meets the $x$-axis at $N$. The shaded region is enclosed by the curve, the $x$-axis and the line $QN$.
parts.label: b

subparts.text: Write down the $x$-coordinate of $N$.
subparts.label: i

subparts.text: Kai Ming says that the area of the shaded region is the value of $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{k} -2\tan 2x\,dx$, where $k$ is the $x$-coordinate of $N$. Explain why he is wrong.
subparts.label: ii
subparts.answer: The shaded region lies below the $x$-axis, so the integral has a negative value, and an area cannot be negative.

subparts.text: Use your answer to part (a) to find the exact area of the shaded region.
subparts.label: iii

figure.description: Cartesian axes with origin labelled $O$, horizontal axis labelled $x$ and vertical axis labelled $y$. Show mainly the fourth quadrant (x from 0 to about 0.75, y from about 0.5 down to about -5). Draw the curve $y = -2\tan 2x$ for $0 \le x < \pi/4$: it starts at $O$ and falls ever more steeply as $x$ increases, heading downwards towards (but never reaching) the vertical line $x = \pi/4$; label the curve '$y = -2\tan 2x$'. Do not draw or label the asymptote. Draw the horizontal straight line $y = -2$ across the diagram, labelled '$y = -2$'; it meets the curve at the point $Q$, which is at $(\pi/8, -2)$ — mark $Q$ with a dot and the letter $Q$ only (no coordinates printed). Draw a vertical line segment from $Q$ straight up to the $x$-axis, meeting it at the point $N$ at $(\pi/8, 0)$; label it $N$ just above the axis (no coordinate printed). Shade the region enclosed by the $x$-axis from $O$ to $N$, the segment $NQ$, and the curve from $O$ to $Q$ (this region lies entirely below the $x$-axis). Do not print any numerical values on the axes.

It keeps the source's structure and method but changes the function (double angle, tangent from the origin), the region (closed by a vertical line QN) and the answer, so it is a twin and not the source re-numbered; only light wording edits remain.
fixes: Stem of (b): replace 'which starts at the origin O' with 'which passes through the origin O'.
(b)(i): 'Write down' asks for a short solve of tan 2x = 1; use 'State the x-coordinate of N' or 'Find', to match the 1 mark.
Solution (b)(iii): show the line -ln(1/sqrt 2) = ln sqrt 2 before (1/2) ln 2, so the sign change is seen.
verdict.key_verdict: The setter's key and the blind examiner agree on every part, and my own working of (b)(iii) confirms (1/2) ln 2.

gen_meta.method_note: Source: differentiate ln(sin x) by the chain rule to get cot x, then reverse it to find an area that lies below the x-axis (integral negative, take its size); twin: differentiate ln(cos 2x) to get -2 tan 2x, then reverse it the same way for a below-axis region under y = -2 tan 2x.

question_text:
The diagram shows three places in a nature reserve joined by straight footpaths: the visitor centre $A$, a bird hide $B$ and a jetty $C$.
The bird hide $B$ is $215$ m from $A$ on a bearing of $132^\circ$.
The jetty $C$ is $168$ m from $B$, and the bearing of $B$ from $C$ is $196^\circ$.

parts.label: a

parts.text: Calculate the bearing of $A$ from $C$.
parts.label: b

parts.text: The diagram below is a scale drawing of the footpaths $AB$, $BC$ and $CA$, drawn to a scale of $1$ cm to $20$ m.
parts.label: c

subparts.text: On the diagram, construct the perpendicular bisector of $AB$.
subparts.label: i
subparts.answer: Perpendicular bisector of $AB$ constructed, with construction arcs shown.

subparts.text: A rest shelter, $T$, is to be built so that it is the same distance from the footpath $AB$ as from the footpath $AC$. By making a suitable construction, show the possible positions of $T$ on the diagram.
subparts.label: ii
subparts.answer: Bisector of angle $BAC$ constructed; $T$ lies on this line.

subparts.text: Given also that $T$ is the same distance from $A$ as from $B$, find the actual distance of $T$ from $C$.
subparts.label: iii

FIGURE 1 (with the stem, not to scale): triangle $ABC$ with straight sides. $A$ is on the left. $B$ is below and to the right of $A$. $C$ is to the right of $A$, almost level with it, and above $B$. Draw a short north arrow (dashed vertical line with 'N') at each of $A$, $B$ and $C$. Label side $AB$ '215 m' and side $BC$ '168 m'. Side $AC$ is drawn but not labelled. At $C$, mark the angle '$196^\circ$' measured clockwise from the north line to $CB$ (a reflex-style bearing arc sweeping past south). No other lengths or angles shown.
FIGURE 2 (for part (c), an accurate scale drawing, scale 1 cm to 20 m, with the caption 'Scale: 1 cm represents 20 m' and one north arrow in a corner): place $A$ on the left. $B$ is $10.75$ cm from $A$ in the direction $132^\circ$ clockwise from north (down and to the right). $C$ is $8.4$ cm from $B$ in the direction $016^\circ$ clockwise from north (almost straight up, slightly right). question_text: A candle maker pours every candle she makes from exactly $864\,\text{cm}^{3}$ of melted wax.

parts.text: One candle is a solid hemisphere. Calculate the radius of this candle.
parts.label: a

parts.text:
Another candle is a solid pyramid with a square base. She slices the pyramid parallel to its base, so that the top part is a small pyramid and the bottom part is a frustum. The volume of the frustum is $608\,\text{cm}^{3}$.
Find the ratio of the height of the frustum to the height of the original pyramid.
parts.label: b

figure.description: Two separate solids side by side, no lengths marked. Left, labelled 'Candle (a)': a solid hemisphere resting on its flat circular face, with its radius drawn from the centre of the flat face to the rim and labelled $r$. Right, labelled 'Candle (b)': a right pyramid on a square base ABCD with apex V directly above the centre of the base. A horizontal dashed slice parallel to the base cuts the edges VA, VB, VC, VD at P, Q, R, S, forming a smaller square PQRS. The small pyramid VPQRS on top is labelled 'small pyramid' and the solid between PQRS and ABCD is labelled 'frustum'. No heights, side lengths or angles are given.

verdict.why: Same sub-skill and method (volume → length via the hemisphere formula; cube root of a similar-solids volume ratio after a parallel cut) with a new context, different solids, non-proportional numbers (864/608 vs 625/585) and a different ratio asked, so it is a genuine twin; clean numbers and teacher-voiced working, only the stem's 'same material for every object' frame stays close to the source. (Aside: the source key's (b) 2/5 looks wrong for the ratio asked — small cone : frustum should be 2 : 3 — worth a look on the bank row.)
fixes: In (b), say 'Find, in the form 1 : n, the ratio of the height of the frustum to the height of the original pyramid' so the answer form is fixed, as a school paper would.
In (a), add 'Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures' or rely on the paper's front-page instruction — keep it consistent with the rest of the set.
Vary the opening sentence away from the source's 'used X cm^3 for each object' frame (e.g. state the wax volume inside each part) so the stem shape is less parallel to the source.
verdict.key_verdict: The setter's key and the blind examiner agree on both parts, and both are correct.

gen_meta.method_note: The source finds a sphere's size from its volume, then takes the cube root of a volume ratio of similar solids (small cone from whole) to compare heights after a parallel cut; the twin does the same with a hemisphere and a square-based pyramid, subtracting the frustum to get the small solid's volume first.

blind_answers.(b): 1 : 3 (small pyramid volume = 864 − 608 = 256; volume ratio 256/864 = 8/27, so linear ratio 2/3; frustum height : original height = 1/3 : 1 = 1 : 3)

question_text: A patient swallows a tablet of a painkiller at 08 00. The amount of the drug, $M$ milligrams, left in her body $t$ hours after she swallows the tablet is given by $M = c \times 2^{-0.25t}$, where $c$ is a constant.

parts.text: The tablet contains 480 mg of the drug. Write down the value of $c$.
parts.label: a

parts.text: Calculate the amount of the drug left in her body at 20 00 on the same day.
parts.label: b

parts.text: A nurse says, "At 08 00 the next morning, the amount of the drug left will be $\frac{1}{16}$ of the amount in the tablet." Show, with working, whether the nurse is right.
parts.label: c
parts.answer: The nurse is not right. At 08 00 the next morning $t = 24$, so $M = c \times 2^{-6} = \frac{1}{64}c$, which is $\frac{1}{64}$ of the amount in the tablet, not $\frac{1}{16}$.

parts.text: On the axes given, sketch the graph of $M = c \times 2^{-0.25t}$ for $0 \le t \le 12$. Use your answers to parts (a) and (b) and mark the values clearly on the axes.
parts.label: d
parts.answer: Smooth decreasing exponential curve from $(0, 480)$ on the $M$-axis to $(12, 60)$, getting less steep as $t$ increases and staying above the $t$-axis; $480$ marked on the $M$-axis, $12$ on the $t$-axis and $60$ on the $M$-axis.

figure.description: A blank pair of axes for the candidate's sketch in part (d), first quadrant only. The horizontal axis is drawn as an arrow pointing right and labelled $t$ at its right end. The vertical axis is drawn as an arrow pointing up and labelled $M$ at its top end. The point where the axes meet is labelled $O$. There are no scale marks, no numbers, no grid and no curve on the axes — the candidate draws the curve and writes the values. The axes are about 8 cm wide and 6 cm tall.

verdict.why: A sound twin: the same read-the-constant, substitute, test-a-claimed-multiple-with-index-laws and sketch-through-two-points structure as the source, but as decay with clock times in a new context, and numbers (480, exponent -0.25t, t = 12 and 24, 1/16 against 1/64) that are not an offset or multiple of the source's. Clean numbers and right weight for 7 marks; only the wording of part (c) is slightly off the examination register.
fixes: Part (c): replace 'Show, with working, whether the nurse is right.' with the usual examination wording, e.g. 'Is the nurse correct? Justify your answer with calculations.'
Stem: say 'The amount of the drug, $M$ mg, in her body $t$ hours after 08 00' so that t is tied to the clock time the later parts use, and the tablet's 480 mg at t = 0 is plainly the starting amount.
verdict.key_verdict: The setter's key and the blind examiner agree on every part, and my own working confirms the values (c = 480, 60 mg, 1/64 not 1/16, decay curve from (0, 480) to (12, 60)).

gen_meta.method_note: The source reads the constant of $P = n \times 2^{0.1t}$ as the starting value, turns dates into $t$, uses index laws to test a claimed multiple, and sketches the exponential through two found points; the twin does the same with a decaying model $M = c \times 2^{-0.25t}$, turning clock times into $t$ and testing a claimed fraction.

blind_answers.(c): Nurse is not right. At 08 00 next morning t = 24, M = 480 x 2^(-6) = 480/64 = 7.5 mg, which is 1/64 of 480, not 1/16 (1/16 of 480 = 30 mg).
blind_answers.(d): Smooth decreasing, concave-up (convex) exponential-decay curve starting on the M-axis at (0, 480) and ending at (12, 60); mark 480 on the M-axis, 60 on the M-axis (or as the end point's height), and 12 on the t-axis; curve stays above the t-axis and does not touch it.

gen_meta.originality_note: New context (a drug leaving the body, clock times instead of years), a decay curve instead of growth, new numbers (480, exponent $-0.25t$, $t = 12$ and $24$, claim $\frac{1}{16}$ against $\frac{1}{64}$) and all sentences rewritten.

question_text: Mei Ling looks after the herb beds in a community garden.

parts.text: In March she sowed seeds of four herbs. The bar chart shows, for each herb, the number of seeds sown and the number of seeds that germinated.
parts.label: a

subparts.text: The germination rate of a herb is the percentage of its sown seeds that germinated. Which herb has the highest germination rate? Show your working.
subparts.label: i

subparts.text: Mei Ling wants the germination rate of basil to reach at least $70\%$. She sows $x$ more basil seeds and assumes that every one of them germinates. Form an inequality in $x$ and solve it to find the least number of basil seeds she must still sow.
subparts.label: ii
subparts.answer: $\frac{22 + x}{38 + x} \geq \frac{70}{100}$, $x \geq 15\frac{1}{3}$, so the least number is $16$

parts.text: Mei Ling wants to sew a grow bag for a young lime tree from a rectangular sheet of canvas measuring $120$ cm by $40$ cm. question_text: Two sets of axes are drawn in the diagram, labelled (i) and (ii). On each set of axes, the point $(1, 3)$ is marked with a black dot.

parts.text: On the axes given, sketch the following graphs. Show any points where the graph meets the axes, and label any asymptotes.
parts.label: a
parts.answer: (i) Hyperbola $y = \frac{3}{x}$ in the first and third quadrants through $(1, 3)$ and $(-1, -3)$, axes as asymptotes. (ii) Exponential curve $y = 3^{x}$ through $(0, 1)$ and $(1, 3)$, approaching the $x$-axis as $x \to -\infty$.

subparts.text: $y = \frac{3}{x}$
subparts.label: i
subparts.answer: Two branches, in the first and third quadrants, through $(1, 3)$ and $(-1, -3)$; no intercepts; the $x$-axis and $y$-axis are asymptotes.

subparts.label: ii
subparts.answer: Increasing curve with $y$-intercept $(0, 1)$, through $(1, 3)$, always above the $x$-axis and approaching it as $x \to -\infty$.

parts.text: Hence explain why $x = 1$ is the only solution of the equation $x\left(3^{x}\right) = 3$.
parts.label: b
parts.answer: $x(3^{x}) = 3$ can be written as $3^{x} = \frac{3}{x}$. For $x < 0$, $\frac{3}{x} < 0$ while $3^{x} > 0$, so the graphs do not meet. For $x > 0$, $y = 3^{x}$ increases while $y = \frac{3}{x}$ decreases, so they meet only once, at $(1, 3)$. Hence $x = 1$ is the only solution.

Each has a horizontal x-axis marked from -3 to 3 and a vertical y-axis marked from -6 to 6, with integer tick marks, arrowheads on the positive ends, the axes labelled x and y, and the origin labelled O. On each set of axes a single black dot is drawn at the point (1, 3), labelled (1, 3). No curves are drawn; the axes are left blank for the candidate's sketch.

verdict.key_verdict: The setter's key and the blind examiner agree on every part, and both are correct.

For x < 0, y = 3^x is positive but y = 3/x is negative, so the graphs do not meet. For x > 0, y = 3^x is increasing while y = 3/x is decreasing, so they can intersect at most once, and they meet at (1, 3). Hence x = 1 is the only solution.
